modules.name: bootstrap-and-load
modules.purpose: Turn a bare PHP request into a fully initialized WordPress runtime: locate configuration, verify host requirements, define constants, connect the database, start the object cache, load plugins and the theme, hand off to the request handler.

business_rules.description: PHP < 7.4 or missing mysqli (with no db.php drop-in) aborts the request before any WordPress code runs.
A .maintenance file whose $upgrading timestamp is older than 600 seconds is ignored, so a crashed upgrade cannot lock the site permanently.
SHORTINIT truthy stops the boot immediately after the object cache and default filters.
An unrecognized WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE silently becomes 'production'.
Plugins recorded as fatal in paused-extension storage are skipped on subsequent requests.
pluggable.php loads after all plugins, enabling plugins to redefine wp_mail(), wp_authenticate() and other pluggable functions.
Initial post types and taxonomies are registered twice: at wp-settings.php:566 and again on the init hook.
The child theme's functions.php loads before the parent theme's.
An uninstalled site is redirected to wp-admin/install.php before most of core loads.
The fatal error handler is registered before the database connects, so DB failures remain recoverable.

algorithms.name: config discovery
algorithms.description: Two-location search for wp-config.php with a guard preventing a nested WordPress from stealing its parent's config.

algorithms.name: maintenance window self-heal
algorithms.description: Four sequential escape conditions; a stale .maintenance older than 10 minutes is ignored.

algorithms.name: memoized whitelist resolution
algorithms.description: Environment type and development mode both resolve once into a static and fall back to a safe default on any unrecognized value.

algorithms.name: paused-extension filtering
algorithms.description: Plugins/themes that fataled are removed from the active list before loading.

findings.finding: Boot order is a public contract: 311 requires in fixed sequence with six named checkpoints. Cannot be refactored without breaking the plugin ecosystem.
No autoloader for core. Every request pays the cost of loading the whole codebase; SHORTINIT is the only mitigation.
Four drop-ins (advanced-cache.php, object-cache.php, db.php, sunrise.php) replace core subsystems by filename convention with no interface validation.
Recovery mode is armed before the DB connects, making it capable of surviving almost any failure.
wp_magic_quotes() re-slashes superglobals; all WordPress input arrives slashed and wp_unslash() must be called before use. A pervasive correctness trap.

modules.name: hooks-plugin-api
modules.purpose: The extension mechanism the entire system is built on. Provides the action and filter engine through which 565 actions and 1638 filters are dispatched, plus plugin lifecycle registration.

business_rules.description: Default priority is 10; lower runs earlier. A null priority becomes 0.
Default accepted_args is 1. Callbacks receive a sliced argument list when they accept fewer args than passed.
A callback whose unique id cannot be built is silently dropped with no error or notice.
Within one priority, callbacks run in registration order.
Re-registering the same callback at the same priority overwrites rather than duplicating.
Registering a hook while it is executing re-sorts the live iteration; equal-priority additions still run in that pass, lower-priority ones do not.
In an action every callback receives the original arguments; in a filter each receives the previous callback's return value as args[0].
A filter callback that returns nothing returns null, which becomes the filtered value.
register_uninstall_hook() rejects instance-method callbacks because the callback is serialized into the uninstall_plugins option.
Callbacks registered on the 'all' hook fire before every hook dispatch in the system.
apply_filters_deprecated() emits its notice only when a callback is actually registered.
has_filter() returns the integer priority when a specific callback is found; falsy comparison against priority 0 is a known trap.

algorithms.name: callback unique id
algorithms.description: String callbacks key by name; objects by spl_object_id; [obj,method] by spl_object_id+method; [Class,method] by Class::method; anything else returns null and is dropped.

algorithms.name: live iteration re-sort
algorithms.description: Repositions PHP's internal array pointer for each active nesting level when a hook is added during its own dispatch.

algorithms.name: three-branch argument dispatch
algorithms.description: accepted_args==0 uses call_user_func; >= num_args uses call_user_func_array with full args; otherwise array_slice. Avoids array_slice when possible.

algorithms.name: symlink-aware plugin basename
algorithms.description: arsort over $wp_plugin_paths so the longest canonical path matches first, then strips WP_PLUGIN_DIR/WPMU_PLUGIN_DIR.

findings.finding: Actions and filters share one implementation; do_action() is apply_filters() with the return discarded. The distinction is a single boolean.
Closures cannot practically be removed once registered because their key is spl_object_id(). Structural limitation with no core workaround.
resort_active_iterations() depends entirely on PHP internal array pointer semantics; the most fragile code in the kernel, with no test coverage available in this tree.
Silent failure on unbuildable callback ids means a typo'd add_filter() produces no diagnostic.
The 'all' hook check runs on every dispatch site (~3371) even when unused.
Because 1638 filters wrap core values, no core function's return value can be specified without also specifying its filters. The single most important constraint on writing accurate WordPress specs.
spl_object_id reuse after garbage collection could theoretically collide two callbacks within a request; no guard exists.

modules.name: database-wpdb
modules.purpose: The entire data access layer. A single ~4230-line class with no ORM, no query builder and no server-side prepared statements. Every module reaches the database through the global $wpdb.

fields.name: tables
fields.value: posts, comments, links, options, postmeta, terms, term_taxonomy, term_relationships, termmeta, commentmeta

fields.name: ms_global_tables
fields.value: blogs, blogmeta, signups, site, sitemeta, registration_log, sitecategories

fields.name: incompatible_modes
fields.value: NO_ZERO_DATE, ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, STRICT_TRANS_TABLES, STRICT_ALL_TABLES, TRADITIONAL, ANSI

business_rules.description: prepare() adds its own quoting; callers must not wrap %s in quotes. Pre-existing quotes are stripped.
An argument used as both %i identifier and %s value is a hard error: _doing_it_wrong() and prepare() returns null.
Placeholder/argument count mismatch triggers _doing_it_wrong(); too few args returns empty string which query() refuses.
%f is always rewritten to %F so float formatting is locale-independent.
Every executed SQL string passes through apply_filters('query', $query).
A write containing text the target column's charset cannot represent is rejected outright, never truncated.
On MySQL error 2006 (server gone away) the query is retried exactly once after reconnection.
check_connection() retries 5 times with 1-second sleeps, blocking the request for up to ~5 seconds.
Charset utf8 is always upgraded to utf8mb4; utf8_general_ci becomes utf8mb4_unicode_ci, upgraded further to utf8mb4_unicode_520_ci when supported.
Six strict SQL modes (NO_ZERO_DATE, ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, STRICT_TRANS_TABLES, STRICT_ALL_TABLES, TRADITIONAL, ANSI) are stripped on connect.
A failed INSERT/REPLACE resets insert_id to 0 so a stale id cannot leak.
$where in update()/delete() supports only equality joined with AND; no OR and no operators.
Blog-scoped table names are recomputed by set_blog_id(); global and ms-global tables are not.
If the connection is lost after template_redirect has fired, wpdb fails silently rather than emitting an error page into a partial response.

algorithms.name: prepare() placeholder interpolation
algorithms.description: sprintf-derived: strips caller quotes, escapes stray percents, preg_split with stride 3, classifies %s/%d/%f/%F/%i, checks identifier-vs-value conflicts and arity, then escapes and interpolates.

algorithms.name: placeholder escape sentinel
algorithms.description: Per-request hash_hmac sentinel replaces literal % in values; a query filter at priority 0 restores it just before execution, blocking second-order placeholder injection.

algorithms.name: charset upgrade cascade
algorithms.description: utf8 -> utf8mb4; utf8_general_ci -> utf8mb4_unicode_ci; -> utf8mb4_unicode_520_ci when the server supports it.

algorithms.name: invalid text rejection
algorithms.description: Per-column charset and byte length are read via SHOW FULL COLUMNS and memoized; unrepresentable writes are refused rather than mangled. check_ascii() is the fast path.

algorithms.name: reconnect with backoff
algorithms.description: DO 1 liveness probe, then 5 retries with sleep(1); silent failure after template_redirect.

findings.finding: prepare() is string interpolation, not a server-side prepared statement. Every SQL-injection defense in WordPress rests on this one regex-driven function.
The 'query' filter lets any plugin rewrite every SQL statement in the system, bypassing every guard above it.
$allow_unsafe_unquoted_parameters remains true for backward compatibility, preserving the historically unsafe %1$s-as-identifier pattern. The class docblock itself calls it risky.
strip_invalid_text_* issues extra SHOW FULL COLUMNS queries per table on first use; correctness bought with round-trips.
5x1s reconnect sleeps inside a web request is a latency cliff under DB stress; requests queue rather than fail fast.
No transaction API. wpdb exposes no begin/commit/rollback, so multi-table operations such as deleting a post and its meta are not atomic.
$queries profiling only populates when SAVEQUERIES is defined, so production query analysis requires a code change.
The db.php drop-in can replace this class entirely with no enforced interface contract: a 4200-line implicit interface.

modules.name: options-and-transients
modules.purpose: WordPress's key-value store. Site configuration, plugin settings, cached remote data and expiring values all live in wp_options addressed by name. Read on every request via wp_load_alloptions(), making its caching behavior the largest single lever on WordPress performance.

fields.name: _transient_timeout_{name}
fields.type: option row holding the unix expiry

business_rules.description: Option names are trimmed; an empty name returns false.
blacklist_keys and comment_whitelist are transparently remapped to disallowed_keys / comment_previously_approved with a deprecation notice.
'alloptions' and 'notoptions' are protected names; writing to them calls wp_die().
update_option() returns false when the value is unchanged, making 'no change' indistinguishable from 'failure'.
Updating an option that does not exist delegates to add_option().
An option whose serialized value exceeds 150000 bytes (filterable via wp_max_autoloaded_option_size) is automatically set to auto-off.
An explicit on/off autoload value is never overridden by the automatic heuristic; only auto, auto-on and auto-off are re-evaluated.
A transient without an expiration is autoloaded; with an expiration it is not.
Transient expiry is lazy: enforced on read, plus a scheduled delete_expired_transients() sweep.
With a persistent object cache present, transients never touch the database.
A transient whose value row exists but whose timeout row is missing is deleted and recreated.
get_option('home') returning an empty string falls back to get_option('siteurl').
Object values are cloned before storage so later caller mutation cannot alter what was saved.
The wp_autoload_values_to_autoload filter can only remove values from the valid set, never add new ones (array_intersect guard).
Every option write passes through sanitize_option($option, $value).

algorithms.name: five-level option read cascade
algorithms.description: pre_option filters -> alloptions bulk cache -> notoptions negative cache -> per-option object cache -> single-row SELECT. Misses are recorded in notoptions so they never re-query.

algorithms.name: automatic autoload sizing
algorithms.description: Serialized values over 150000 bytes are demoted to auto-off, protecting every request from a single oversized autoloaded option.

algorithms.name: two-row transient with lazy expiry
algorithms.description: Value and timeout stored as separate option rows; expiry checked on read, both rows deleted when stale. Repairs a missing timeout row by recreating both.

algorithms.name: autoload-as-expiry-proxy
algorithms.description: get_transient() uses presence in alloptions to infer the transient has no timeout, avoiding a timeout lookup. Couples the autoload flag to transient semantics.

findings.finding: wp_options is the most contended table in WordPress: configuration, plugin settings, transient cache and expiry timestamps share one key-value table with one unique index.
autoload as a 6-valued enum rather than a boolean preserves the distinction between human decision and heuristic, so the heuristic never overrides intent.
update_option() returning false for 'unchanged' is a persistent source of caller bugs with no way to distinguish it from a write failure.
Transients silently change storage backend based on the presence of a persistent object cache: a real testing hazard between production and default installs.
Transient expiry has no guaranteed upper bound; without read traffic or the cron sweep, expired rows persist indefinitely.
The 150KB autoload-size heuristic is a mitigation, not a fix: hundreds of options just under the limit still bloat every request.
pre_option_{option} allows a plugin to fully replace any option read without touching the database, making any option's value unspecifiable in isolation.

modules.name: cache-and-object-cache
modules.purpose: A request-scoped in-memory cache designed to be transparently replaced by a persistent one via the object-cache.php drop-in. The default implementation does not persist across requests.

business_rules.description: The default object cache is request-scoped only; nothing survives the response.
Under multisite, keys in non-global groups are prefixed with '{blog_id}:'; global groups are not.
An invalid key (not int, not non-empty string) fails with _doing_it_wrong() and returns false.
A cached null is a genuine hit, distinguished from a miss by the array_key_exists() arm of _exists().
Objects are cloned on set() and again on get(), two clones per round trip.
$expire is accepted and ignored by the default implementation.
add() respects wp_suspend_cache_addition(); set() does not.
An empty $group becomes 'default'.
counts, plugins, theme_json and themes are declared non-persistent groups.
get() sets the by-reference $found parameter, the only reliable way to distinguish a cached false from a miss.

algorithms.name: multisite key prefixing
algorithms.description: Non-global-group keys get '{blog_id}:' prepended. The entire multisite cache isolation mechanism is a string prefix.

algorithms.name: null-safe existence check
algorithms.description: isset() OR array_key_exists() so a cached null is a hit, not a miss.

algorithms.name: double clone isolation
algorithms.description: Objects cloned on both set and get so caller mutation cannot corrupt the in-process cache array.

findings.finding: The default cache being non-persistent means most WordPress installs run with no real caching; performance observed on a default install does not transfer to one with Redis or Memcached.
The object-cache.php drop-in is an implicit interface with no formal contract; cache-compat.php exists to polyfill drop-ins predating newer methods.
Cache correctness for false and null depends on callers using $found; callers checking 'if (false === $value)' re-query on every legitimately-false cached value.
Multisite cache isolation is a string prefix, so a drop-in ignoring switch_to_blog() leaks data across sites.
Double-cloning every cached object is measurable overhead in object-heavy paths, paid because the cache is a live in-process array.

modules.name: metadata
modules.purpose: The generic attribute system. One implementation serves posts, comments, terms, users and blogs, driven by a $meta_type string that resolves to a table name.

business_rules.description: $meta_type resolves to '{type}meta' on $wpdb; an unknown type returns false and aborts the operation.
Meta keys and values are wp_unslash()ed on write because input arrives slashed.
$unique = true is enforced by SELECT COUNT(*) before insert with no unique index, so concurrent writers can both succeed.
A meta key is protected when its key, stripped of every character that is not printable ASCII or a Unicode letter, begins with underscore.
All meta for an object is cached as a single entry; reading one key loads them all.
$single = true returns values[0]; false returns the full array.
Every meta value passes sanitize_meta(), dispatching to the subtype-specific filter when one is registered.
Values are maybe_serialize()d on write and maybe_unserialize()d on read, so arrays and objects round-trip transparently.
The add_/get_/update_/delete_{meta_type}_metadata filters returning non-null fully replace the operation.
update_meta_cache() orders by meta_id ASC (umeta_id for users), preserving insertion order for multi-value meta.

algorithms.name: string-driven table dispatch
algorithms.description: _get_meta_table() builds '{type}meta' and looks it up as a wpdb property; the object id column is sanitize_key('{type}_id'). Whitelist by property existence.

algorithms.name: non-atomic unique check
algorithms.description: SELECT COUNT(*) then INSERT with no unique index on (object_id, meta_key).

algorithms.name: bulk meta cache priming
algorithms.description: One query with WHERE {column} IN (ids) ORDER BY meta_id ASC, grouped into array<id, array<key, value[]>>. The N+1 defense used by WP_Query.

algorithms.name: anti-smuggling protected-key check
algorithms.description: Strips every non-printable-ASCII, non-letter character before testing for a leading underscore, so invisible-character prefixes cannot bypass protection.

algorithms.name: three-function default resolution
algorithms.description: get_metadata / get_metadata_raw / get_metadata_default split so registered defaults can be returned without the raw reader knowing about the registry; bridged by filter_default_metadata().

findings.finding: Five entity types share one code path parameterized by a string that becomes a SQL table name; a bug here is a bug in every entity type at once.
No unique index backs $unique = true. The guarantee is advisory and duplicate meta rows are a known real-world outcome.
meta_value is LONGTEXT with no index, so every meta_query is a scan or a meta_key-only join. The root cause of most slow WordPress queries.
Whole-object meta caching turns any single-key read into a full meta load: a win in loops, a loss for objects with large meta sets.
The underscore-prefix protection is enforced only in UI and REST layers, never at the storage layer. Protected meta is a display convention, not access control.
The character-stripping in is_protected_meta() is a deliberate anti-smuggling measure, indicating this check has been attacked before.

modules.name: posts-and-post-types
modules.purpose: The central content entity. wp_posts stores posts, pages, attachments, revisions, nav menu items, reusable blocks, templates, global styles and fonts: 16 built-in types in one table distinguished only by the post_type column.

fields.name: post_name
fields.note: the slug; max 200 bytes including -N suffix

fields.name: guid
fields.note: seeded from get_permalink() on first publish, never updated

fields.name: supports
fields.note: title, editor, author, thumbnail, excerpt, trackbacks, custom-fields, comments, revisions, page-attributes, post-formats

business_rules.description: A publish status with a post_date_gmt at least 60 seconds in the future is silently converted to 'future'.
A future status whose date is less than 60 seconds away is silently converted to 'publish'.
An attachment must have status inherit, private, trash or auto-draft.
Drafts store post_date_gmt as 0000-00-00 00:00:00, requiring MySQL NO_ZERO_DATE mode to be off.
Slugs are not generated or uniqued for draft, pending or auto-draft statuses.
Attachment slugs must be unique across all post types; hierarchical types are unique within (type, parent); flat types within the type.
Slugs matching a registered feed name, 'embed', a pagination number, or a date-archive segment are forced to take a numeric suffix.
Slugs are truncated to 200 bytes inclusive of the -N suffix via _truncate_post_slug().
Every status change fires transition_post_status and the dynamic {old}_to_{new} action.
The guid column is populated from get_permalink() on first publish and never updated afterwards.
Any status transition unconditionally clears the publish_future_post cron event, guarding against a future->draft bounce.
nav_menu_item and user_request bypass slug uniqueness entirely.

algorithms.name: status derived from date
algorithms.description: publish with a date >= 60s ahead becomes future; future with a date < 60s away becomes publish. Status is not caller-controlled.

algorithms.name: three-scope slug uniqueness
algorithms.description: attachments unique across all types; hierarchical types unique within (type, parent) including attachments; flat types unique within type. Reserved names (feeds, 'embed', pagination numbers, date-archive segments) force a suffix. do-while loop with one query per iteration.

algorithms.name: dynamic transition hooks
algorithms.description: do_action("{old_status}_to_{new_status}") generates up to 121 undeclared hook names from the 11 built-in statuses.

algorithms.name: transition side effects
algorithms.description: GUID seeding on first publish, lastpostmodified/lastpostdate cache invalidation across three timezones, post-count cache invalidation, and unconditional publish_future_post cron clearing.

findings.finding: Sixteen semantically unrelated entities share one table and one code path. wp_posts is not a posts table; it is WordPress's generic object store.
Post status is a derived attribute computed from post_date_gmt at write time; any specification treating status as caller-controlled is wrong.
Slug uniqueness uses a query-per-iteration loop with no unique index: slow at scale and racy under concurrency, the same pattern as add_metadata()'s $unique.
The {old}_to_{new} dynamic hook creates up to 121 undeclared hook names that cannot be enumerated by static analysis.
The guid column is documented as a permanent identifier yet seeded from a permalink, the root of long-standing feed-reader confusion.
NO_ZERO_DATE must be stripped from MySQL's SQL mode because drafts store zero dates: two modules' constraints are causally locked together.
post.php is 298 KB in a single file with no class boundary for most of its logic, the largest single unit of coupling in the codebase.

modules.name: query-and-loop
modules.purpose: Turn a URL into a set of posts. WP parses the request into query variables, WP_Query compiles those into SQL, and The Loop iterates the result. WordPress's front controller, router and query layer combined.

fields.name: public_query_vars
fields.note: settable from the URL query string

fields.name: private_query_vars
fields.note: settable only in PHP; includes post_status, post__in, fields, perm

business_rules.description: The do_parse_request filter returning false skips request parsing, the main query and 404 handling entirely.
Private query vars such as post_status, post__in and fields can never be set from the URL. This is the boundary that keeps drafts private.
Admin, robots.txt and favicon requests never 404.
?page=N on a post whose content lacks <!--nextpage--> is a 404.
The posts page never honors <!--nextpage--> pagination; any page var there produces a 404.
An empty author, term or post-type archive returns 200 if the queried object exists; an empty paged archive always 404s.
The split-query optimization applies only when no filter altered the SQL and either a persistent object cache exists or posts_per_page < 500.
found_posts is computed with SELECT FOUND_ROWS() only when a LIMIT is present and no_found_rows is false.
Search terms that are single a-z or dash characters, or locale stopwords, are dropped. Quoted terms keep their surrounding spaces to signal exact-match intent.
Post, meta, term and author caches are primed once, on the first the_post() of a loop.
have_posts() fires loop_end and rewinds automatically at the end of a loop; an empty result fires loop_no_results.
Every SQL clause is filterable twice (early and as *_request) and posts_pre_query can replace the query altogether.

algorithms.name: 404 exemption cascade
algorithms.description: Default is to 404. Exemptions for admin/robots/favicon, for found posts with valid pagination, and for empty archives whose queried object exists. Paged empty archives are never exempt.

algorithms.name: seven-clause SQL assembly with double filtering
algorithms.description: fields, join, where, groupby, orderby, distinct and limits are each filterable early and again as *_request, plus posts_clauses and posts_request over the whole set. 34 filters total.

algorithms.name: split query
algorithms.description: SELECT ID then hydrate individually from cache, instead of SELECT wp_posts.*. Only for unfiltered queries with either a persistent object cache or posts_per_page < 500.

algorithms.name: SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS pagination
algorithms.description: found_posts read via SELECT FOUND_ROWS(); max_num_pages = ceil(found_posts / posts_per_page). Forces MySQL to count the full match set.

algorithms.name: stopword-filtered LIKE search
algorithms.description: Terms are trimmed, single a-z/dash tokens and stopwords dropped, survivors become leading-wildcard LIKE conditions. No index usable, no ranking.

algorithms.name: lazy loop cache priming
algorithms.description: On the first the_post() only, reduce results to ids and bulk-prime post, term, meta and author caches. The loop-level N+1 defense.

findings.finding: WP_Query::get_posts() exposes 34 filters. The generated SQL is a default, not a specification; any statement about what WordPress queries is conditional on the plugin set.
The public/private query-var split is the boundary keeping drafts private. It is enforced by two array literals and add_query_var() can breach it in one line.
SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS is on by default, so every archive page counts the entire matching set to render a pager. The most common WordPress scalability failure.
Core search is LIKE '%term%' with a stopword filter: no index usable, no ranking. Any real search requirement needs an external engine.
The split-query optimization silently disables itself when any plugin filters the SQL, so adding one filter changes the query shape, not just its clauses.
404 determination happens after the main query has already run, so a 404 page has paid for a full post query.
WP_Query is simultaneously a router result, a query builder, an iterator and a state machine for 25+ is_*() conditionals: the most overloaded class in WordPress.

modules.name: taxonomy-and-terms
modules.purpose: Classify objects via a three-table design (wp_terms, wp_term_taxonomy, wp_term_relationships) that separates the word from the classification from the assignment. The most normalized part of the WordPress schema and the source of its most confusing API.

fields.name: term_group
fields.note: synonym grouping via alias_of; vestigial

fields.name: term_taxonomy_id
fields.note: the id that actually links to objects

fields.name: parent
fields.note: no foreign key; cycles possible

fields.name: count
fields.note: direct assignments only; hierarchical rollup computed at read time

business_rules.description: Objects are linked by term_taxonomy_id, never term_id. One term_id may serve several taxonomies.
The term name is validated for emptiness twice: before and after sanitization.
A null description is coerced to empty string to avoid a database error.
A non-existent parent term id rejects the insert with the missing_parent error.
Duplicate detection happens after insert; only a row with a lower term_id counts as the duplicate, and the newly inserted rows are then deleted.
In wp_set_object_terms(), a non-existent term passed as a string is created; passed as an integer it is silently skipped.
Assigning a term already related to the object is a no-op, checked with one query per term.
With $append = false, terms present before but absent from the new list are removed.
Term counts can be deferred with wp_defer_term_counting(true) and accumulate in a static keyed by taxonomy.
A taxonomy's update_count_callback overrides the default counting query.
Hierarchical count padding counts only objects with post_status = 'publish'.
Count padding deduplicates by object id, so a post in both a child and its parent is counted once for the parent.
Ancestor walking has an explicit cycle guard against corrupted parent chains.
alias_of groups terms via term_group, allocated as MAX(term_group) + 1.

algorithms.name: insert-then-detect-duplicate
algorithms.description: Rows are inserted first, then a SELECT looks for an older row (term_id < new id) with the same slug/parent/taxonomy. If found, the new rows are deleted and the pre-existing ids returned. A compensating transaction implemented without transactions.

algorithms.name: type-dependent term creation
algorithms.description: In wp_set_object_terms() a string term that does not exist is created via wp_insert_term(); an integer term that does not exist is skipped with no error.

algorithms.name: static-accumulator deferred counting
algorithms.description: wp_defer_term_counting(true) queues term ids in a static array keyed by taxonomy, flushed in one pass by wp_update_term_count($x,$y,true).

algorithms.name: hierarchical count padding
algorithms.description: One join over term_relationships x posts filtered to publish status, building term_items[term_id][object_id]; ancestors are walked with a cycle guard and object ids copied up, deduplicating so a post in child and parent counts once.

algorithms.name: term_group aliasing
algorithms.description: alias_of joins an existing group or allocates MAX(term_group)+1 and moves the target term into it.

findings.finding: The term_id / term_taxonomy_id split is correct normalization that the API then obscures: most functions take term_id while relationships use tt_id. The module's dominant defect source.
wp_insert_term() inserts before checking for duplicates and deletes its own rows on conflict: a compensating transaction implemented without transactions, which wpdb does not provide.
String-creates / integer-skips in wp_set_object_terms() is an undocumented type-dependent behavior difference with no error signal.
Term assignment costs one existence query per term, so bulk assignment is O(n) queries.
Hierarchical counts are computed at read time by _pad_term_counts(), so a large category tree pays a term_relationships x posts join on every render.
The cycle guard in ancestor walking is evidence that corrupted parent chains occur in practice; the schema has no foreign key preventing them.
term_group / alias_of is a vestigial synonym feature with no UI, superseded in practice by term meta.

modules.name: comments
modules.purpose: Accept, moderate and display reader responses plus trackbacks and pingbacks. The moderation pipeline is the most rule-dense business logic in WordPress core: a spam filter expressed as option-driven sequential checks.

fields.name: comment_karma
fields.note: legacy; no core consumer

fields.name: comment_approved
fields.note: NOT a boolean: '1','0','spam','trash','post-trashed'

fields.name: comment_type
fields.note: comment | pingback | trackback

business_rules.description: A duplicate (same post, parent, author, email and content, excluding trashed comments) is rejected with HTTP 409.
Users with manage_options or moderate_comments are never flood-throttled.
Flood detection looks back one hour, matched by user_id when logged in, otherwise by IP, or by email in either case.
The flood verdict defaults to false; core supplies only the query and the comment_flood_filter hook. No rate limit is enforced by core itself.
The post author and any user with moderate_comments are auto-approved without any moderation check.
comment_moderation = '1' holds every comment and short-circuits all other moderation rules.
A comment containing comment_max_links or more '<a ... href' occurrences is held.
Each moderation_keys entry is matched case-insensitively with Unicode as a substring against author, email, URL, content, IP and user agent.
comment_previously_approved = '1' requires a prior approved comment, matched by user_id for registered users or by author name AND email otherwise.
A disallowed-list match overrides any approval and sets the status to 'trash' if EMPTY_TRASH_DAYS is truthy, otherwise 'spam'.
Over-length comment fields return WP_Error with HTTP status 200, not 400.
comment_approved is a varchar with values 1, 0, spam, trash, post-trashed.
Comment counts can be deferred and flushed in one pass, using the same static-accumulator pattern as term counts.
The final approval value always passes through the pre_comment_approved filter, so a plugin can override the entire pipeline's verdict.

algorithms.name: duplicate detection
algorithms.description: Concatenated prepare() fragments matching post, parent, author, optional email and exact content, excluding trashed comments. A hit terminates with HTTP 409.

algorithms.name: flood window query with defaulting-false verdict
algorithms.description: One-hour lookback keyed on user_id or IP, OR email; the verdict is delegated to comment_flood_filter which core never sets true.

algorithms.name: four-rule moderation
algorithms.description: Manual moderation short-circuit, link-count threshold, keyword substring match across six fields, previously-approved requirement.

algorithms.name: post-decision disallowed override
algorithms.description: The disallowed list runs after the approval decision and overrides it, choosing trash or spam based on EMPTY_TRASH_DAYS.

findings.finding: Core ships no working rate limit. wp_check_comment_flood() performs a query then asks a filter that defaults to false; the feature reads as protection but provides none without a plugin.
Moderation keywords match as unquoted substrings across six fields including IP and user agent, so short keywords produce heavy false positives.
The disallowed list overrides the approval decision after it is made, so pipeline ordering rather than rule content determines the outcome.
Whether a disallowed comment becomes trash or spam depends on EMPTY_TRASH_DAYS, an unrelated constant; disabling trash silently changes spam handling.
comment_approved as a string mixing booleans and state names forces every consumer to string-compare, with endemic '0' == false traps.
Length validation is inconsistent: two fields use mb_strlen(v,'8bit') and two use strlen(). Both count bytes, but the asymmetry suggests character counting was intended in the first pair.
Moderation inspects text already filtered by comment_text, so a rendering plugin can inadvertently change what the spam filter sees.

modules.name: media-and-attachments
modules.purpose: Upload handling, image resizing, responsive image markup and media metadata. The largest body of pure algorithmic code in WordPress: geometry, aspect-ratio matching and srcset generation.

business_rules.description: WordPress never upscales: a requested size larger than the original returns false and the original is used.
Cropping uses max() of the width/height ratios, producing a cover-fit source rectangle rather than a letterboxed one.
An invalid $crop value falls back to ['center','center'].
Aspect-ratio matching tolerates a 1-pixel difference because integer rounding during resize makes exact matches rare.
srcset candidates wider than 2048px (max_srcset_image_width filter) are excluded unless the candidate is the src image itself.
srcset candidates must live in the same directory as the source file.
The image editor is chosen per operation by testing availability, mime-type support and required methods, preferring Imagick then GD.
The editor choice is memoized under an md5 of (args, implementations) in the global image_editor cache group.
Responsive attributes (srcset, sizes, loading, decoding, fetchpriority) are injected at render time into output HTML, not stored in post content.
Every upload generates one file per registered subsize.

algorithms.name: cover-fit crop geometry
algorithms.description: size_ratio = max(new_w/orig_w, new_h/orig_h) yields a source rectangle covering the destination box; offsets from left/right/top/bottom keywords or centered with floor().

algorithms.name: upscale prevention
algorithms.description: Three-branch guard on which destination dimensions were supplied; any request larger than the original returns false.

algorithms.name: fuzzy aspect matching
algorithms.description: Scale the larger image down to the smaller one's width, then compare within a 1px tolerance via wp_fuzzy_number_match().

algorithms.name: srcset candidate filtering
algorithms.description: Same-directory guard, is_src detection, 2048px width cap with an is_src exemption, and fuzzy ratio match.

algorithms.name: capability-negotiated editor selection
algorithms.description: Loop over Imagick then GD, testing test(), supports_mime_type() and required methods; memoized by md5 of args plus implementations.

findings.finding: The most algorithmically dense module in core and one of the few with genuinely non-trivial mathematics; the crop geometry is correct and well-guarded.
Storage grows multiplicatively with registered sizes: N subsizes per upload, with no deduplication and no lazy generation in core.
The 1-pixel fuzzy match is a workaround for rounding in the resize pipeline, meaning aspect-ratio identity is approximate throughout the media layer.
Injecting responsive attributes at render time means the same stored content produces different HTML across WordPress versions: good for upgrades, bad for output reproducibility.
The wp_image_editors filter can substitute an arbitrary class into the image pipeline with only duck-typed test() and supports_mime_type() checks.

modules.name: embeds-oembed
modules.purpose: Turn a bare URL on its own line into rich embedded content, and expose WordPress's own posts as oEmbed providers.

fields.name: post_parent
fields.type: the post the embed appears in

business_rules.description: A URL alone on its own line is auto-embedded; a URL inline in a paragraph is not.
59 built-in providers are matched by regex before any network request is made.
Discovery only runs when no registered provider matches and discovery is enabled for the request.
JSON is attempted first, XML second.
XML parsing disables external entity loading (XXE defense).
Embed results are cached as oembed_cache post-type rows keyed by URL plus args.
Newlines are stripped from provider HTML so wpautop() cannot insert paragraph tags inside it.
photo-type responses are rendered by WordPress as an img tag; rich and video responses inject the provider's own HTML.

algorithms.name: provider registry match
algorithms.description: 59 pattern => [endpoint, is_regex] pairs matched with preg_match; sanitize_provider() validates each entry.

algorithms.name: link-rel discovery fallback
algorithms.description: HTTP GET the target URL and scrape <link rel="alternate" type="application/json+oembed"> or its XML variant. A server-side request to a user-supplied URL.

algorithms.name: format negotiation
algorithms.description: _fetch_with_format('json') then fall back to 'xml'.

algorithms.name: type-dispatched rendering
algorithms.description: photo renders a validated img tag; video and rich inject provider html; link renders an anchor.

findings.finding: Discovery makes a server-side HTTP request to a user-supplied URL; its safety depends entirely on the HTTP API's SSRF guards, not on anything in this module.
rich and video responses inject third-party HTML into the page. The trust boundary is the provider allowlist, so the 59-entry registry rather than sanitization is the actual security control.
Explicitly disabling XXE in _parse_xml() is one of the few places core defends against a parser-level attack.
Using a post type as the embed cache means embed data participates in post queries, revisions and exports.

modules.name: users-roles-capabilities
modules.purpose: The authorization model. Roles are named bundles of capabilities, capabilities are booleans, and a meta-capability layer translates object-specific questions into concrete capability checks. This is WordPress's entire access control.

default_roles.name: administrator
default_roles.scope: full site control including manage_options, edit_users, activate_plugins, edit_plugins, edit_themes, install_plugins, update_core, unfiltered_html

default_roles.name: editor
default_roles.scope: all content by anyone: edit_others_posts, delete_others_posts, manage_categories, moderate_comments, unfiltered_html

default_roles.name: author
default_roles.scope: own content with publishing: publish_posts, edit_published_posts, delete_published_posts, upload_files

default_roles.name: contributor
default_roles.scope: own content only; cannot publish and cannot upload files

business_rules.description: has_cap() requires ALL mapped capabilities, not any one of them.
do_not_allow is unset from the user's capability set before evaluation, so a requirement for it can never be satisfied. It is the deny primitive.
A multisite super admin passes every check unless the mapped capability list contains do_not_allow.
Every user implicitly holds the 'exist' capability.
map_meta_cap() returning an empty array means the action is allowed with no requirements, because array_all over an empty array is true.
A user with ID < 1 cannot edit any user, not even themselves.
Any user may edit themselves via edit_user with their own id (empty caps emitted).
In multisite, editing a super admin requires being a super admin, and any user edit requires manage_network_users.
A user may not remove themselves in multisite unless they are a super admin.
delete_post / delete_page without a post argument emits _doing_it_wrong() and returns do_not_allow: fail closed.
Numeric capabilities are legacy user levels, translated to capabilities with a deprecation notice.
install_languages, resume_plugin, resume_theme and view_site_health_checks are granted dynamically by user_has_cap callbacks, never stored.
Roles are stored per user in wp_usermeta under {prefix}capabilities, so role membership is per site in multisite.
get_super_admins() prefers the $super_admins PHP global over the site_admins network option.
Contributors can neither publish posts nor upload files.

algorithms.name: meta capability mapping
algorithms.description: An ~870-line switch translating object-specific meta capabilities (edit_post, delete_post, edit_user, remove_user) into lists of primitive capabilities based on the object's author, status and type.

algorithms.name: five-stage capability check
algorithms.description: map_meta_cap first, super-admin bypass second, user_has_cap filter third, do_not_allow removal fourth, then require ALL mapped caps.

algorithms.name: dynamic capability grants
algorithms.description: Three core callbacks on user_has_cap compute environment-dependent capabilities rather than storing them.

algorithms.name: incremental role definition
algorithms.description: populate_roles() calls eight version-named functions (_160 through _300), layering each historical WordPress version's capability additions.

findings.finding: The user_has_cap filter can rewrite the entire capability array on any check, so every authorization decision in WordPress is overridable by any plugin in one line.
map_meta_cap() is an ~870-line switch that is the sole source of truth for object-level permissions, with no formal specification: the code is the policy.
'Empty caps array means allowed' is a dangerous default for a permission system; a map_meta_cap case that falls through without emitting a capability grants access silently.
The 6.1 hardening of delete_post to fail closed when the object argument is missing implies earlier versions failed open in that path.
level_0 through level_10 capabilities persist in every role two decades after deprecation, and plugins still test them.
Roles are stored as user meta with no referential integrity to their definitions; deleting a role leaves users holding a name that resolves to nothing.
Role definitions are spread across eight populate_roles_*() functions ordered by historical version; there is no single place stating what an Editor can do.
$super_admins as a PHP global outranking the database option means a compromised wp-config.php or any early-loading plugin can grant itself total control.

modules.name: authentication-and-sessions
modules.purpose: Prove identity and maintain it across requests: password hashing, cookie-based sessions, session tokens, nonces, and the pluggable-function override mechanism.

fields.name: hmac
fields.type: hash_hmac sha256 of user_login|expiration|token keyed by wp_hash(user_login|pass_frag|expiration|token, scheme)

business_rules.description: 35 security functions in pluggable.php can be wholly replaced by any plugin defining them first, because pluggable.php loads after all plugins.
Passwords longer than 4096 bytes hash to '*', which never verifies. A DoS guard expressed as a permanently failing hash.
bcrypt passwords are pre-hashed with HMAC-SHA-384 using key 'wp-sha384', base64-encoded, and prefixed with $wp to survive bcrypt's 72-byte truncation.
Three password hash formats coexist: $P$ (phpass), $2y$ (vanilla bcrypt), $wp$2y$ (WordPress pre-hashed bcrypt).
The auth cookie HMAC key includes a 4-character fragment of the password hash, so changing the password invalidates every outstanding cookie.
The password fragment is substr(hash, 8, 4) for $P$ and $2y$ hashes and substr(hash, -4) otherwise.
Cookie HMACs are compared with hash_equals() for constant-time comparison.
AJAX and POST requests receive a one-hour cookie-expiry grace period.
Cookie lifetime is 14 days with remember-me and 2 days without; in remember-me mode the browser cookie outlives the HMAC expiration by 12 hours.
The logged_in cookie is only marked secure when the auth cookie is secure AND the home URL uses HTTPS.
Cookie validation order is expiry, then user existence, then HMAC, then session token.
Nonce lifetime is 24 hours (nonce_life filter), ticking every 12 hours; both the current and previous tick are accepted.
wp_verify_nonce() returns 1 (0-12h old), 2 (12-24h old) or false, never true.
A nonce is 10 hex characters taken from offset -12 of a wp_hash() result, roughly 40 bits.
Nonces bind to the session token, so logging out invalidates outstanding nonces.
Logged-out users all share uid 0 for nonce generation unless the nonce_user_logged_out filter supplies an identity.

algorithms.name: bcrypt pre-hashing
algorithms.description: base64(hmac_sha384(password, 'wp-sha384')) fed to password_hash(), prefixed '$wp'. Preserves entropy beyond bcrypt's 72-byte limit with domain separation and no null bytes.

algorithms.name: two-stage cookie HMAC
algorithms.description: wp_hash(user_login|pass_frag|expiration|token, scheme) derives a per-user key; that key HMAC-SHA256s user_login|expiration|token. The password fragment is never transmitted but changing it invalidates all cookies.

algorithms.name: half-life nonce ticks
algorithms.description: tick = ceil(time() / (nonce_life/2)); verification accepts tick and tick-1, returning 1 or 2 to signal age. Nonces are deterministic within a 12-hour window.

algorithms.name: pluggable override
algorithms.description: Every function wrapped in if (! function_exists()); pluggable.php loads after all plugins so any plugin can replace the entire security core.

findings.finding: The entire authentication stack is pluggable with no interface contract, so 'how does WordPress authenticate?' is unanswerable without knowing the plugin set.
Password-fragment-in-key-derivation gives password-change-invalidates-sessions without any server-side session store; a stolen cookie survives exactly until the password changes.
Nonces are deterministic within a 12-hour window, making them CSRF tokens rather than nonces; they are replayable within that window.
wp_verify_nonce() returning 1/2/false is a truthiness trap: === true always fails and the stale-nonce signal (2) is almost universally discarded.
40 bits of nonce entropy is adequate for CSRF given action and user binding but far below what the name suggests.
All logged-out users share a single nonce value per action, so anonymous-facing nonces provide no per-user CSRF protection by default.
The bcrypt pre-hashing scheme is a careful, correct solution to the 72-byte truncation, handling both domain separation and null-byte avoidance.
The one-hour POST/AJAX grace period silently extends session validity precisely for state-changing requests, a usability decision with an undocumented security cost.

modules.name: themes-and-templates
modules.purpose: Choose which PHP or HTML file renders the current query, and manage theme registration, parent/child inheritance and theme features.

fields.name: headers
fields.type: array (Theme Name, Template, Version, Requires at least, Requires PHP)

business_rules.description: template_redirect fires only when wp_using_themes() is true.
A HEAD request exits immediately after template_redirect unless the exit_on_http_head filter says otherwise.
robots, favicon, feed and trackback requests are handled before the hierarchy and even when themes are disabled.
The 17 template conditionals are evaluated in a fixed order and the first match wins; is_404 is tested second.
Matching is_attachment removes the prepend_attachment content filter.
No conditional match falls back to index.php.
The template type is sanitized with preg_replace to [a-z0-9-] before becoming part of a filename.
Lookup order per filename is child theme, then parent theme only if a child is active, then wp-includes/theme-compat/.
The first filename in the candidate list that exists anywhere wins, so filename specificity outranks theme proximity.
A urldecoded template-name variant is added to the candidate list only when it differs from the raw name.
A post's custom template slug from post meta is used only if validate_file() returns 0.
After the template_include filter the path must resolve via realpath(), end in .php or .html, and be an existing readable file.
Every template type exposes a {type}_template_hierarchy filter over its candidate list.
Block themes get a final override via locate_block_template().

algorithms.name: ordered conditional hierarchy
algorithms.description: 17 is_* conditionals tested in a fixed order; the first true one selects its getter, which builds a most-specific-first candidate filename list.

algorithms.name: three-location template lookup
algorithms.description: For each candidate filename in order: child theme path, parent theme path (only when a child is active), then wp-includes/theme-compat/. Breaks on first hit, so filename specificity beats location.

algorithms.name: conditional urldecode variant
algorithms.description: A percent-decoded filename candidate is inserted only when decoding actually changes the string, avoiding duplicate candidates for ASCII slugs.

algorithms.name: post-filter inclusion guard
algorithms.description: realpath() resolution, .php/.html extension allowlist, is_file and is_readable checks after template_include, preventing local file inclusion via the filter.

findings.finding: The template hierarchy is not a data structure but the evaluation order of 17 conditionals plus per-type candidate arrays; it cannot be introspected, only read.
template_include returns a filesystem path that is then included; the four-check guard after it is load-bearing security, not defensive style.
Filename specificity beating theme location means a child theme cannot override a parent's more-specific template with a less-specific one.
Child functions.php loads before the parent's while child templates are found before the parent's: two opposite orderings for the same relationship, each correct for its purpose.
theme-compat/ is a third, largely invisible template source that most theme developers never learn about.
validate_file() on the meta-supplied template slug is the only thing stopping post meta from selecting an arbitrary file.

modules.name: rewrite-and-permalinks
modules.purpose: Two inverse operations: compile a permalink structure into regex rules mapping URLs to query variables, and generate URLs from objects. WordPress's router.

fields.name: queryreplace
fields.value: year= monthnum= day= hour= minute= second= name= p= author_name= pagename= s=

business_rules.description: rewritecode, rewritereplace and queryreplace are positionally aligned arrays; compilation substitutes by index with nothing enforcing the alignment.
%pagename% uses a non-greedy ([^/]+?) because pages are hierarchical; %postname% uses greedy ([^/]+); %search% uses (.+) and may contain slashes.
Built-in feed slugs are feed, rdf, rss, rss2 and atom.
pagination_base is 'page' and comments_pagination_base is 'comment-page'.
The full rewrite rule set is stored in the single 'rewrite_rules' option.
An empty rewrite_rules option triggers immediate regeneration.
Any flush_rules() call before wp_loaded is deferred to wp_loaded, so every post type and taxonomy is registered first.
Deferred hard-flush requests accumulate with logical OR in a static; one hard request makes the eventual flush hard.
A hard flush additionally writes .htaccess or web.config, but only when save_mod_rewrite_rules() / iis7_save_url_rewrite_rules() exist (admin only).
14 EP_* bitmasks control which URL classes an endpoint attaches to.
With use_verbose_page_rules enabled (the default), one rewrite rule is generated per page.
Rules can be added at the top or bottom of the set via add_rule($regex, $query, $after).

algorithms.name: positional tag substitution
algorithms.description: Each %tag% is replaced by its regex to build the match pattern and by its query key to build the index.php?... target, using three index-aligned arrays.

algorithms.name: single-option rule cache
algorithms.description: The complete rule set is serialized into the rewrite_rules option and read on every permalink request; regeneration is triggered when the option is empty.

algorithms.name: sticky deferred flush
algorithms.description: Flushes before wp_loaded are re-registered on wp_loaded, with a static $do_hard_later accumulating hardness via OR across all deferred callers.

algorithms.name: verbose page rules
algorithms.description: When a structure starts with a variable tag, an explicit rule is emitted per page so pages can be distinguished from posts, making rule count O(pages).

findings.finding: The rewrite compiler is three positionally-aligned arrays; inserting a tag requires editing all three at the same index and nothing enforces the alignment.

The entire routing table is one serialized option row read on nearly every request and subject to the autoload size heuristic; large sites can push it past 150 KB and silently de-autoload their own router.
use_verbose_page_rules makes rule count O(pages), so a site with thousands of pages has a rewrite option measured in megabytes.
Flush deferral to wp_loaded means flush_rewrite_rules() never does what its name says at call time, a persistent source of confusion.
Hard flushes silently become soft on the front end because save_mod_rewrite_rules() is only defined in the admin.
pagination_base couples this module to wp_unique_post_slug(): changing it would change which post slugs are legal.

modules.name: script-modules-and-assets
modules.purpose: Register, resolve dependencies for, and emit scripts and stylesheets. Two generations coexist: the classic WP_Dependencies handle system and WP_Script_Modules with ES modules and import maps.

business_rules.description: A handle with an unregistered dependency is dropped from output entirely.
The missing-dependency _doing_it_wrong() notice fires at most once per handle per request, tracked in a private array.
Inside recursion a resolution failure returns false and aborts that branch; at the top level it skips only that handle and continues.
set_group() only ever moves a handle to a lower group number: footer to header, never the reverse.
Group 0 is the header and group 1 the footer.
A handle already in done is never re-emitted.
A '?' suffix on a handle is stripped before resolution and re-applied to the emitted URL.
Script-module fetch priority is derived from a module's dependents via dependents_map, not from its own declaration.
Script modules emit a browser import map plus modulepreload links for static dependencies.
Both registries use the same register -> enqueue -> to_do -> done lifecycle.

algorithms.name: recursive topological dependency resolution
algorithms.description: all_deps() walks handles, computes missing deps via array_diff against the registry, recurses into declared deps, and appends survivors to to_do. Failure aborts a branch during recursion but only skips one handle at the top level.

algorithms.name: monotonic group promotion
algorithms.description: set_group() writes only when the new group is strictly lower than the recorded one, so a handle can move footer->header but never header->footer.

algorithms.name: dependents-derived fetch priority
algorithms.description: get_highest_fetchpriority() consults dependents_map so a module used by a high-priority module inherits urgency.

algorithms.name: once-per-handle warning
algorithms.description: Missing-dependency notices are recorded in a private array so repeated resolutions do not spam the log.

findings.finding: The footer-to-header promotion rule makes $in_footer advisory: any header-loaded dependent silently pulls a script into the head.
A missing dependency causes silent omission rather than an error; before the 6.9.1 notice there was no diagnostic at all.
There is no explicit cycle detection in all_deps(); circular dependencies rely on the queued/group short-circuits and can otherwise recurse to the stack limit.
Two complete asset systems coexist with no shared abstraction; a dependency cannot span the classic and module registries.
script-loader.php is a 4000-line hand-maintained registry with versions as string literals, the only place bundled JS versions can be discovered.
Computing fetch priority from dependents is a genuinely modern touch: a module used by a high-priority module inherits urgency automatically.

modules.name: widgets-and-nav-menus
modules.purpose: Two legacy content-placement systems that predate blocks and remain load-bearing: sidebar widgets and navigation menus.

fields.name: id_base
fields.note: class-level identifier

fields.name: number
fields.note: which placed instance

fields.name: id
fields.note: {id_base}-{number}

fields.name: option_name
fields.note: widget_{id_base}; ALL instances share one option row

fields.name: _menu_item_object_id
fields.type: int referenced post or term id

fields.name: _menu_item_menu_item_parent
fields.type: int parent MENU ITEM id, not post_parent

fields.name: _menu_item_orphaned
fields.type: timestamp; set when the referenced object is gone

fields.name: menu_order
fields.type: int on the post row; drives ordering

business_rules.description: All instances of a widget class share one option row named widget_{id_base}, keyed by instance number.
A widget instance id is {id_base}-{number}.
Form field names are widget-{id_base}[{number}][{field}] so one submission carries every instance.
update() is responsible for sanitization; core does not sanitize widget input on the widget's behalf.
is_preview() reports whether rendering occurs inside the Customizer.
A menu is a nav_menu taxonomy term; a menu item is a nav_menu_item post.
Menu-item semantics live in nine _menu_item_* meta keys, not in post columns.
Menu hierarchy uses _menu_item_menu_item_parent, not post_parent.
Menu ordering uses the menu_order column on the post row.
An item whose referenced object is deleted is marked _menu_item_orphaned rather than removed.
An empty post_title falls back to the referenced object's title at render time.

algorithms.name: multi-instance single-option storage
algorithms.description: One WP_Widget subclass serves many placed widgets; all instance settings live in one option row keyed by number, with _register() iterating stored numbers to call _register_one().

algorithms.name: meta-driven menu item model
algorithms.description: A menu item's type, target object, parent and presentation all live in nine post meta rows; the post row itself carries only ordering and an optional title override.

algorithms.name: orphan tombstoning
algorithms.description: _menu_item_orphaned flags items whose referenced object was deleted, standing in for a foreign key the schema lacks.

findings.finding: The one-option-per-widget-class model means every instance is loaded whenever any one is read, and a corrupt entry affects all instances.
Sanitization is delegated to third-party update() implementations, making widget input the least uniformly-validated data path in core.
Menu items store their meaning in nine meta rows each; a 50-item menu is 50 posts and roughly 450 meta rows, which is why menus are a documented performance concern.
Two parallel parent columns exist on the same row and only one is used; any tool reasoning about post_parent for menu items is wrong.
_menu_item_orphaned is a manual tombstone standing in for the foreign key the schema lacks, the same pattern as the taxonomy cycle guard.

modules.name: customizer
modules.purpose: Live-preview theme and site settings with a changeset that can be saved, scheduled or discarded. Superseded by the Site Editor for block themes but still the settings surface for classic themes.

fields.name: type
fields.note: theme_mod | option | custom

fields.name: capability
fields.note: PER-SETTING authorization

fields.name: theme_supports
fields.note: only registered if the theme declares this support

fields.name: transport
fields.note: refresh | postMessage

fields.name: validate_callback
fields.note: returns WP_Error to reject

business_rules.description: Each setting declares its own capability, defaulting to edit_theme_options. Authorization is per-field, not per-screen.
A setting with theme_supports set is only registered when the theme declares that support.
transport is 'refresh' by default; 'postMessage' requires the theme to supply JS for live updates.
validate_callback rejects with WP_Error, sanitize_callback cleans, sanitize_js_callback prepares the preview value: three separate hooks.
Settings store to theme_mod (theme-scoped) or option (site-wide), selected by $type.
Unsaved Customizer state persists in a customize_changeset post identified by a UUID, making previews shareable and schedulable.
The Customizer registers its controls on wp_loaded, then fires customize_register.
Theme previewing begins at setup_theme, before the theme's own functions.php context is final.

algorithms.name: four-level registry
algorithms.description: Panel contains Section contains Control which writes Setting; controls are UI and settings are storage, in a many-to-many relationship.

algorithms.name: changeset as a post
algorithms.description: Unsaved state is serialized into a customize_changeset post keyed by UUID rather than a session, enabling shareable preview links and scheduled publication.

algorithms.name: three-stage value pipeline
algorithms.description: validate_callback rejects, sanitize_callback cleans for storage, sanitize_js_callback prepares for the JS preview.

findings.finding: Per-setting capabilities make the Customizer the most granular authorization surface in WordPress, finer than the admin screens it configures.
Storing unsaved state as a post makes previews shareable and schedulable at the cost of customize_changeset rows accumulating in wp_posts.
A 198 KB manager class with a roughly 1000-line register_controls() is the second-largest single unit of coupling after post.php.
The Customizer, widgets and nav menus are three overlapping settings surfaces that the block editor partially replaces without removing any of them; core carries all four.

modules.name: block-editor
modules.purpose: Parse, register and render the block-based content format. Post content is HTML with block boundaries encoded as HTML comments; this module turns that string into a tree and back.

fields.name: blockName
fields.note: null for freeform

fields.name: innerContent
fields.note: strings are literal HTML; nulls are inner-block placeholders

fields.name: render_callback
fields.note: presence makes the block dynamic

business_rules.description: Block boundaries are HTML comments, so block content renders correctly without any parsing.
An omitted namespace in a block delimiter defaults to core/.
Void blocks (ending /-->) carry no inner content and are emitted without a stack push.
Text outside any delimiter becomes a core/freeform block.
Unclosed blocks at end of document are closed implicitly; the parser never fails.
innerContent mixes strings (literal HTML) and nulls (inner-block placeholders).
Serialization substitutes each null in innerContent with the next serialized inner block, in order.
Block metadata resolves from a pre-built manifest first, then block.json on disk, then $args.
Blocks under wp-includes/ are treated as core and skip the file_exists() check.
Core blocks get implicit wp-block-{name} style and wp-block-{name}-editor editorStyle handles, plus wp-block-{name}-theme when wp-block-styles is supported.
Registration returns false when neither the metadata nor $args supplies a name.
A block with a render_callback is dynamic; its output is computed at render time rather than read from stored content.

algorithms.name: comment-delimited format
algorithms.description: Structure encoded as HTML comments so content degrades gracefully; namespace optional and defaulting to core/; open/close, void and freeform forms.

algorithms.name: possessive-quantifier JSON brace matcher
algorithms.description: The attrs sub-pattern uses *+ with two lookaheads to match a JSON object containing } characters, stopping at the } preceding the comment terminator, without catastrophic backtracking.

algorithms.name: stack-machine parsing with implicit recovery
algorithms.description: proceed() dispatches on token type; no-more-tokens with a non-empty stack closes every open block implicitly, so parsing never fails.

algorithms.name: null-placeholder serialization
algorithms.description: innerContent records the block's own HTML as strings and its children's positions as nulls; serialize_block walks the array substituting each null with the next serialized inner block, giving lossless round-tripping.

algorithms.name: three-source metadata resolution
algorithms.description: Pre-built manifest via WP_Block_Metadata_Registry, then block.json decode, then $args; core blocks detected by path prefix skip file_exists entirely.

findings.finding: Storing structure in HTML comments means the canonical content format degrades gracefully: an install with the block editor disabled still renders every post correctly. The best design decision in the block system.
The attribute regex is a hand-rolled JSON brace matcher with a possessive quantifier; content structure is parsed by regular expression, bounding attribute complexity.
The parser cannot fail: every malformed input maps to freeform or implicit closure, so there is no validation stage and no error signal for corrupt block markup.
The innerContent null-placeholder design is what makes lossless round-tripping possible; without it nesting position would have to be inferred.
The metadata manifest exists because reading 115 block.json files per request was measurably slow: a performance workaround visible in the public API surface.
Dynamic blocks make stored content an incomplete description of the page; two installs with identical post_content can render differently.

modules.name: blocks-library
modules.purpose: The 115 built-in blocks. Each is a block.json plus, for dynamic blocks, a PHP render callback.

stats.note: 88 = 86 required by require-dynamic-blocks.php + legacy-widget.php + widget-group.php. The 92 PHP files in blocks/ include index.php, blocks-json.php and require-dynamic-blocks.php, which are not blocks.

business_rules.description: Every core block is defined by a block.json file.
All core block.json contents are inlined into blocks-json.php as a single 206 KB PHP array, collapsing 115 file reads into one require.
Blocks with a PHP file are dynamic; those without render from saved markup.

The 'missing' block preserves the original content when a block type is not registered. It is a STATIC block — wp-includes/blocks/missing/ contains only block.json; the placeholder is rendered client-side by the editor, not by PHP.

The 'freeform' block wraps pre-block classic editor content. It is a STATIC block — wp-includes/blocks/freeform/ contains block.json and editor CSS only. The wrapping happens in blocks.php, not in a render callback.
Post-context blocks (post-title, post-content, etc.) read from the current query context rather than from attributes.

findings.finding: A 206 KB generated PHP array is loaded to avoid 115 file reads; core traded memory on every request against I/O on every request.
88 of 115 core blocks (76.5%) are dynamic, counted from require-dynamic-blocks.php. The block system stores markup for only 27 blocks; for the rest, output is computed at render time.
The missing block is a graceful-degradation mechanism preserving content when a block-providing plugin is deactivated, the block equivalent of _menu_item_orphaned.
Blocks now cover comments, queries, navigation and site identity, functionality previously owned by templates, widgets and menus: four systems expressing the same capabilities.

modules.name: block-supports
modules.purpose: Cross-cutting block features. A block declares supports in block.json and this module injects the resulting classes and inline styles at render time, so no block implements colour or spacing handling itself.

fields.name: block_to_render
fields.note: global state threading the current block through the pipeline

business_rules.description: Supports apply only to blocks with a registered block type; unregistered blocks receive nothing.
Attributes contributed by multiple supports are space-concatenated, with the first writer taking the slot and later ones appending.
Non-scalar values and booleans are skipped entirely; the explicit is_bool() check prevents true stringifying to '1' in markup.
A support without an apply callback contributes nothing at render time, though it may still register attributes.
Attributes pass through prepare_attributes_for_render() so schema defaults are applied before any support sees them.
The block currently being rendered is tracked in the public static $block_to_render.

algorithms.name: space-concatenation attribute merge
algorithms.description: Each support's apply callback returns attributes; scalars (excluding booleans) are appended space-separated to any existing value for the same attribute name, letting 23 modules compose without coordination.

findings.finding: The space-concatenation merge makes 23 independent modules composable without coordination, but registration order affects emitted class order.
The explicit is_bool() exclusion is a bug fix visible in the code: is_scalar() alone would have injected '1' into markup.
$block_to_render as a public static means block rendering is not reentrant at the supports layer without saving and restoring it.

modules.name: global-styles-theme-json
modules.purpose: A declarative styling system. theme.json describes settings (what the editor offers) and styles (what is applied), merged across four origins and compiled to CSS.

fields.name: PRESETS_METADATA
fields.note: presets become CSS custom properties AND utility classes

fields.name: PROPERTIES_METADATA
fields.note: style path to CSS property mapping

fields.name: PROTECTED_PROPERTIES
fields.note: properties the user origin may not override

fields.name: ELEMENTS
fields.value: link, heading, h1-h6, button, caption, cite

business_rules.description: The four origins merge strictly in order default, blocks, theme, custom; later origins override earlier ones.
get_merged_data($origin) stops the cascade at the named origin, enabling 'what would the theme alone produce?' queries.
User global styles are stored as one wp_global_styles post per theme, created on first access.
The user global-styles post id is memoized in a static for the request.
PROTECTED_PROPERTIES cannot be overridden by the user origin.
The root CSS custom-property selector is :root and the root block selector is body.
Presets generate both CSS custom properties and utility classes per PRESETS_METADATA.
Viewport breakpoints are validated and normalized to pixels before becoming media queries.
Styleable elements are link, heading, h1 through h6, button, caption and cite.
WP_Theme_JSON_Schema migrates older theme.json versions forward at load time.

algorithms.name: four-origin cascade with early exit
algorithms.description: merge core, then block, then theme, then user data, returning early at the requested origin so callers can obtain pre-user-customization state.

algorithms.name: schema-as-constants
algorithms.description: Valid settings, styles, properties, protected properties, elements and pseudo-selectors are all declared as class constants: a formal data model expressed in PHP arrays.

algorithms.name: viewport breakpoint validation
algorithms.description: is_valid_viewport_breakpoint_size, get_viewport_breakpoint_value_in_pixels and sanitize_viewport_settings validate theme-supplied breakpoints before they become media queries.

findings.finding: The only genuinely declarative subsystem in WordPress: everything else is imperative PHP with hooks, while theme.json is data compiled to CSS.
A 216 KB class that is mostly schema constants is effectively a specification written as PHP arrays, the closest thing in core to a formal data model.
The four-origin cascade with early exit lets every consumer ask 'what would this be without user edits?', which makes non-destructive reset possible.
Storing user styles as a post per theme means switching themes silently switches style sets, and wp_global_styles posts accumulate for uninstalled themes.
theme.json is theme-supplied data that becomes CSS media queries, so the viewport validation chain is a real injection boundary rather than schema tidiness.

modules.name: style-engine
modules.purpose: Convert style objects into CSS rules. A small, focused module that both block supports and global styles depend on.

fields.name: declarations
fields.note: sanitized on add

business_rules.description: Declarations are sanitized when added, not when rendered.
Multiple named rule stores can coexist and are rendered independently.
The processor deduplicates and combines rules before output.
WP_Style_Engine exposes both class names and inline styles for the same style object.

algorithms.name: named rule stores
algorithms.description: Block supports, global styles and layout each accumulate rules in independent named stores, rendered together and deduplicated by the processor.

findings.finding: The best-factored module in core: single responsibility per class, no globals, no hooks in the hot path.
Returning either a class name or an inline style for the same input is what lets block supports choose between preset utility classes and custom values.

modules.name: html-api
modules.purpose: Parse and modify HTML correctly in PHP without a DOM. Two layers: a streaming tag-level editor and a full HTML5-spec-compliant tree-construction parser.

business_rules.description: WP_HTML_Tag_Processor never constructs a tree; modifications are byte-level and applied on get_updated_html().
Scanning is forward-only; set_bookmark() and seek() are the only way to revisit a position.
get_attribute_names_with_prefix() enables attribute discovery by prefix, which the Interactivity API depends on.
WP_HTML_Processor implements HTML5 tree construction including the stack of open elements and the list of active formatting elements.
Fragment parsing requires a context element, defaulting to <body>.
Unsupported constructs raise WP_HTML_Unsupported_Exception rather than producing incorrect output.
get_breadcrumbs() and matches_breadcrumbs() provide ancestor querying without a DOM or XPath.

algorithms.name: streaming byte-level editing
algorithms.description: Forward-only scan recording queued replacements applied on get_updated_html(); memory proportional to the document, not to a node graph.

algorithms.name: bookmark and seek
algorithms.description: Named positions saved during a forward scan allow non-linear editing on a forward-only cursor.

algorithms.name: HTML5 tree construction
algorithms.description: Insertion modes, stack of open elements, list of active formatting elements and the adoption agency algorithm, per the HTML5 specification.

findings.finding: The most rigorous code in WordPress: a genuine HTML5 tree-construction implementation totalling 384 KB, written because regex-based HTML manipulation caused a long tail of correctness and security bugs.

Failing loudly via WP_HTML_Unsupported_Exception is the opposite of the block parser's never-fail design: two parsers in one codebase with deliberately opposite error philosophies, each right for its input.
The streaming tree-free design keeps memory proportional to the document, necessary for wp_filter_content_tags() running on every post.
Neither processor is exposed as a simple 'modify this HTML' helper; callers must drive the cursor, which keeps it fast and makes it easy to misuse.

modules.name: interactivity-api
modules.purpose: Declarative client-side interactivity driven by data-wp-* HTML attributes, with server-side pre-rendering of directives so the initial HTML is already correct.

business_rules.description: State and config are namespaced per store and serialized into the page for client hydration.
Directives are processed server-side so the initial HTML already reflects state.
Each directive handler is invoked on both entering and leaving an element, enabling correct context push and pop around nested elements.
A directive value may be namespace::path; without a namespace it resolves against the enclosing data-wp-interactive.
Kebab-case attribute suffixes are converted to camelCase state keys.
Setting one style property via data-wp-style preserves all other inline styles on the element.
References support a ! negation prefix, resolved in evaluate().

algorithms.name: server-side directive processing
algorithms.description: Walk the HTML with the directives processor, dispatching each recognized data-wp-* attribute to a handler called on both element entry and exit so context frames push and pop correctly.

algorithms.name: namespaced reference resolution
