algorithms.description: parse_directive_name splits directive from suffix; extract_directive_value parses namespace::path with a default namespace; evaluate() walks namespace then path honouring a ! negation prefix.

algorithms.name: non-destructive style merging
algorithms.description: merge_style_property parses the existing style attribute, replaces one property and re-serializes, so directives compose with author-written inline styles.

findings.finding: Server-side directive processing means an interactive block's initial render is correct without JavaScript: genuine progressive enhancement, in marked contrast with the React-only editor.
The whole system rests on the HTML API's attribute-prefix discovery; without get_attribute_names_with_prefix() this would be regex-based again.
Directives are HTML attributes containing a small expression language evaluated on both server and client, and the two evaluators must agree.
merge_style_property() reveals that directives compose with author-written inline styles rather than replacing them, required for correctness but easy to overlook when specifying behavior.

modules.name: rest-api
modules.purpose: WordPress's HTTP API. A route registry, a dispatcher with a schema-driven validate/sanitize pipeline, and 49 controllers exposing core entities at /wp-json/.

fields.name: permission_callback
fields.note: ABSENT MEANS PUBLIC; _doing_it_wrong since 5.5.0 but not enforced

fields.name: args
fields.type: array schema driving validate and sanitize

business_rules.description: rest_pre_dispatch returning non-empty bypasses routing, validation, permissions and the callback entirely.
Validation via has_valid_params() runs before sanitization via sanitize_params(); a failure in either skips the callback.
A non-callable handler yields rest_invalid_handler with HTTP 500.
A permission_callback returning false OR null denies the request; forgetting to return is a denial.
A route with no permission_callback skips the permission check entirely and is fully public.
The denial status is 401 for anonymous requests and 403 for authenticated ones, via rest_authorization_required_code().
register_rest_route() called before rest_api_init emits _doing_it_wrong() and the route is not registered.
A missing permission_callback emits _doing_it_wrong() recommending __return_true, but this is a notice and the route still serves.
rest_dispatch_request returning non-null replaces the callback's execution.
$dispatching_requests is a stack, so nested internal dispatches are tracked correctly.
register_route() merges with an existing route unless $override is true.

algorithms.name: validate-then-sanitize dispatch
algorithms.description: match route, verify callable handler, has_valid_params() then sanitize_params(), both schema-driven from the route's args; any failure short-circuits to an error response without invoking the callback.

algorithms.name: fail-closed permission gate
algorithms.description: permission_callback returning false or null denies with 401/403 depending on login state; but an ABSENT callback skips the gate entirely, making the route public.

algorithms.name: reentrant dispatch stack
algorithms.description: $dispatching_requests is pushed on entry and popped at every exit path, allowing nested internal REST requests.

findings.finding: The most consequential rule is that a missing permission_callback means public. The safe default would be denial; instead core warns and serves.
Treating null as denial catches the common 'forgot to return' bug and is the opposite polarity to map_meta_cap()'s 'empty caps means allowed': two authorization layers in core with opposite defaults.
rest_pre_dispatch bypasses the permission check along with everything else, making it a complete authorization bypass by design.

49 controllers plus 5 field classes and 4 search handlers make this the largest specified surface in WordPress and the only subsystem with machine-readable schemas, which is why OpenAPI generation is feasible here and nowhere else.
The schema-driven validate-then-sanitize pipeline is stricter and more uniform than the classic side, where each $_POST handler validates ad hoc.

modules.name: http-api
modules.purpose: Make outbound HTTP requests portably, with a safe variant defending against Server-Side Request Forgery. Underlies updates, oEmbed discovery, feeds, the block directory and every plugin calling a remote service.

business_rules.description: Only wp_safe_remote_* validates the URL; wp_remote_* does not.
Only http and https schemes are accepted.
If wp_kses_bad_protocol() changes the URL in any way it is rejected rather than corrected: sanitization used as detection.
URLs containing userinfo (user:pass@host) are rejected outright.
Hosts containing : # ? [ or ] are rejected, which excludes IPv6 literal addresses entirely.
Requests to the site's own host bypass all IP-range checks so loopback cron and REST self-requests work.
A hostname whose gethostbyname() returns the input unchanged (resolution failure) is rejected.
13 IPv4 ranges are blocked, including 169.254.0.0/16 which the inline comment names as cloud metadata.
A blocked host can be permitted via the http_request_host_is_external filter, which defaults to false.
With an explicit port only 80, 443 and 8080 are allowed, filterable via http_allowed_safe_ports.
A URL with no explicit port passes the port check unconditionally.
Transport is chosen per request between cURL and streams based on capability requirements.
WP_HTTP_BLOCK_EXTERNAL with WP_ACCESSIBLE_HOSTS provides a site-wide egress allowlist.

algorithms.name: layered SSRF validation
algorithms.description: Type and scheme check, sanitize-and-compare round trip, structural rejections (userinfo, special host characters), same-host exemption, DNS resolution with 13 blocked IPv4 ranges, then a three-port allowlist.

algorithms.name: sanitize-as-validator
algorithms.description: wp_kses_bad_protocol() output is compared case-insensitively against the original; any difference rejects the URL rather than using the cleaned form.

algorithms.name: capability-based transport negotiation
algorithms.description: _get_first_available_transport() selects cURL or streams per request based on SSL, proxy and streaming requirements.

findings.finding: The most carefully written security function in WordPress: the range list is annotated with RFC intent and the 169.254.0.0/16 comment names cloud metadata explicitly, evidence of threat-model-driven design.
The sanitize-then-compare pattern (reject if changed rather than use the cleaned value) is the correct way to use a sanitizer as a validator and is rare in the codebase.
Validation is by resolved IP but the request is made by hostname; a DNS entry resolving differently between check and request (DNS rebinding) defeats the guard, and nothing pins the resolved address.
Only IPv4 is range-checked. IPv6 literals are rejected outright, but a hostname resolving to IPv6 is not checked because gethostbyname() returns IPv4 only.
Safety is opt-in by function name, and the API makes the unsafe call the shorter and more obvious one.
The same-host exemption means a site whose home option points at an internal hostname can be used to reach that host.

modules.name: xmlrpc
modules.purpose: The legacy remote API: 78 methods across five protocol families, predating REST by a decade and still enabled by default.

business_rules.description: XML-RPC is enabled by default; disabling requires add_filter('xmlrpc_enabled', '__return_false').
The enable_xmlrpc option is deprecated since 3.5.0; its pre_option and option filters are consulted only for back-compat.
Every method authenticates independently with a username and password passed as XML-RPC parameters; there is no session, token or nonce.
78 methods span the wp, metaWeblog, mt, blogger, pingback and demo families.
pingback.ping fetches a caller-supplied URL server-side, unauthenticated.

algorithms.name: layered enablement resolution
algorithms.description: pre_option_enable_xmlrpc, then option_enable_xmlrpc defaulting to true, then the xmlrpc_enabled filter; the chain exists to respect back-compat filters written against the removed option.

algorithms.name: per-call credential authentication
algorithms.description: Each method receives username and password as parameters and authenticates independently, so credentials traverse the wire on every request with no built-in rate limit.

findings.finding: A 211 KB always-on endpoint accepting credentials on every call is the largest legacy attack surface in WordPress; four of its six method families serve clients that no longer exist.
Per-call credentials with no rate limiting make xmlrpc.php the canonical brute-force target; core supplies no throttle, exactly as with comment flooding.
pingback.ping is a server-side fetch of an attacker-supplied URL, structurally identical to the oEmbed discovery risk but reachable unauthenticated.
REST duplicates nearly all of wp.*; two complete remote APIs are maintained in parallel, one with schemas and permission callbacks and one without.

modules.name: feeds
modules.purpose: Publish content as RSS 2.0, RSS 0.92, RDF and Atom, and consume external feeds via SimplePie.

business_rules.description: Feed requests are handled in template-loader.php before the template hierarchy and even when themes are disabled.
Registered feed slugs are feed, rdf, rss, rss2 and atom.
Feed templates are plain PHP using the standard Loop.
Consumed feeds are fetched through the WordPress HTTP API rather than SimplePie's own transport, via WP_SimplePie_File.
Consumed feed content is sanitized with KSES, replacing SimplePie's own sanitizer.
Feed responses are cached as transients via WP_Feed_Cache_Transient.

algorithms.name: vendored-library integration by substitution
algorithms.description: SimplePie's HTTP transport is replaced by WP_SimplePie_File (routing through the WP HTTP API) and its sanitizer by WP_SimplePie_Sanitize_KSES, so the library's two riskiest behaviors use core's audited implementations.

findings.finding: Routing SimplePie through the WP HTTP API and KSES is exactly the right integration: a vendored library's network access and HTML output are both replaced with core's audited implementations.
Four output formats are maintained for a feature whose consumers have largely consolidated on RSS 2.0 and Atom.
Feed templates being ordinary PHP means a plugin filtering the_content also alters feed output, the most common cause of malformed feeds.

modules.name: sitemaps
modules.purpose: Generate XML sitemaps for search engines from a small provider-based architecture.

business_rules.description: Three built-in providers cover posts, taxonomies and users.
Each sitemap file holds at most 2000 URLs, filterable per object type via wp_sitemaps_max_urls.
An XSL stylesheet is served so the raw XML renders readably in a browser.
Only public post types and public taxonomies are included.
The user provider includes only authors with published posts.

algorithms.name: provider registry with paginated index
algorithms.description: An abstract provider yields URL lists; the registry holds providers; the index builds a sitemap-of-sitemaps paginated at 2000 URLs per file, well under the 50000 protocol limit.

findings.finding: A well-factored module (abstract provider, registry, renderer, one tunable) showing what the rest of core would look like if written today.
The 2000-URL page size is 4% of the protocol maximum, a memory-safety choice producing many more files than necessary on large sites.

modules.name: ai-abilities-connectors
modules.purpose: The newest subsystem: a registry of typed, permission-gated, schema-described abilities that AI agents can discover and invoke, plus a provider-agnostic AI client.

fields.name: category
fields.type: string, must be a registered category

business_rules.description: Ability names must match ^[a-z0-9-]+/[a-z0-9-]+$; a namespace prefix is mandatory.
Re-registering an existing ability fails with _doing_it_wrong() and returns null; there is no silent overwrite.
An ability's category must already be registered before the ability can be registered.
Abilities default to not public and not shown in REST, the opposite of register_rest_route()'s default.
Execution is normalize_input, validate_input, check_permissions, do_execute, validate_output.
Both input and output are validated against JSON Schema.
Permissions are checked after input validation, so a malformed request is rejected before authorization runs.
__wakeup() and __sleep() are overridden on the registry and on abilities as unserialization guards, because these objects hold callables.
The AI client's HTTP goes through the WordPress HTTP API via WP_AI_Client_Http_Client.
Registered abilities are exposed to AI models as callable functions by WP_AI_Client_Ability_Function_Resolver.

algorithms.name: five-stage ability execution
algorithms.description: normalize_input, validate_input against JSON Schema, check_permissions, do_execute, then validate_output against JSON Schema. Output validation is unique in core.

algorithms.name: strict registration
algorithms.description: Mandatory namespace pattern, no overwrite of an existing name, and a category that must already exist; all three fail with _doing_it_wrong() and a null return.

algorithms.name: ability to AI function bridge
algorithms.description: The ability-function resolver turns a registered ability's schemas into an LLM tool definition, so one declaration becomes both a REST endpoint and a model-callable function.

findings.finding: The strictest contracts in WordPress: mandatory namespaces, no overwrite, schema-validated input and output, private-by-default visibility. It reads as if written by people who catalogued core's defaults and chose the opposite each time.
Output validation is unique in core; nothing else verifies that a callback returned what it promised.
Checking permissions after input validation lets an unauthorized caller learn whether their input was well-formed; the reverse order would be more conservative.
The ability-to-AI-function bridge means every registered ability is potentially reachable by an LLM, with permission_callback as the only gate, in a context its author may not have anticipated.
156 PHP files of AI infrastructure ship in core with no counterpart in existing WordPress documentation; any specification written before this release is now incomplete.
Explicit __wakeup()/__sleep() guards show awareness of PHP object-injection risk, a defense core does not apply to most other registries.

modules.name: cron
modules.purpose: Schedule deferred and recurring work. WordPress has no daemon; cron is a queue in an option, drained by piggybacking on incoming HTTP requests.

business_rules.description: All scheduled events live in the single autoloaded 'cron' option.
Event identity is timestamp, then hook, then md5(serialize(args)).
Built-in schedules are hourly, twicedaily, daily and weekly.
A single event duplicating another within a plus-or-minus 10-minute window is rejected.
For an event due within 10 minutes or already past, the lower bound becomes 0 so ALL past identical events count as duplicates, preventing accumulation of a repeatedly-failing event.
Cron cannot spawn while DOING_CRON is defined or the doing_wp_cron query arg is present.
A doing_cron lock more than 10 minutes in the future is discarded as invalid, self-healing against clock skew.
WP_CRON_LOCK_TIMEOUT (60 seconds) prevents spawning more than once a minute regardless of how many events are due.
Spawning aborts when no events are ready or the earliest ready timestamp is in the future.
ALTERNATE_WP_CRON runs cron via a visitor redirect and requires a GET request that is neither AJAX nor XML-RPC.
The default path issues a non-blocking loopback HTTP request to wp-cron.php.
The pre_schedule_event filter can replace scheduling entirely, which is how external cron systems take over.
_get_cron_array() migrates pre-version-2 cron arrays on read via _upgrade_cron_array().

algorithms.name: asymmetric duplicate window
algorithms.description: For events due within 10 minutes or already past, min_timestamp becomes 0 so all past identical events count as duplicates; for far-future events the window is symmetric around the event's own timestamp.

algorithms.name: transient-based spawn lock
algorithms.description: A doing_cron transient holds a microtime float; locks more than 10 minutes ahead are discarded, and WP_CRON_LOCK_TIMEOUT doubles as a one-per-minute rate limit.

algorithms.name: visitor-redirect fallback
algorithms.description: ALTERNATE_WP_CRON redirects the visitor's browser back to the same URI with a marker and runs cron during that second request, trading user latency for reliability on hosts where loopback fails.

findings.finding: Cron only runs when someone visits the site; a site with no traffic executes no scheduled work, which is why DISABLE_WP_CRON plus a real crontab is the standard production configuration.

The lock is a transient, so cross-process correctness depends on a persistent object cache; without one it is a database row with no atomic compare-and-set and two concurrent requests can both acquire it.
All events in one autoloaded option means every request loads the full schedule.
The asymmetric duplicate window is subtle but correct: it prevents unbounded accumulation of a repeatedly-failing event while still allowing legitimate future scheduling.
ALTERNATE_WP_CRON makes a visitor's browser the scheduler, adding a redirect to their request.
Argument identity is md5(serialize($args)), so argument order and type changes silently create distinct events.

modules.name: internationalization
modules.purpose: Translate strings, resolve the active locale, and switch locale mid-request.

business_rules.description: pre_determine_locale returning a non-empty string overrides all other locale sources.
A request-supplied locale is honoured only on wp-login.php, via wp_lang in $_GET or $_COOKIE, because the login form must be translatable before a user exists.
All user-supplied locale values pass sanitize_locale_name() before use, because the locale becomes part of a .mo filesystem path.
The admin and ?_locale=user JSON requests use the user's locale; the front end uses the site locale.
During installation, $_REQUEST['language'] or $GLOBALS['wp_local_package'] supplies the locale.
switch_to_locale() maintains a stack in WP_Locale_Switcher; restore_previous_locale() pops it.
Switching locale reloads every already-loaded textdomain in the new locale.
Translations load from .mo files via POMO or from .l10n.php PHP-array files.
The source English string is the lookup key; _x() adds a context prefix to disambiguate identical strings.

algorithms.name: locale precedence chain
algorithms.description: pre_determine_locale filter, then login-screen wp_lang (the only user-supplied source, sanitized), then user locale for admin and ?_locale=user JSON, then installation language, then the site option.

algorithms.name: stack-based locale switching
algorithms.description: switch_to_locale pushes and reloads all textdomains; restore_previous_locale pops and reloads again.

findings.finding: The login-screen locale is the only user-controlled locale input and it becomes part of a filesystem path, making sanitize_locale_name() a path-traversal boundary rather than a formatting nicety.
Using the English source string as the key means fixing a typo in an English string orphans every translation of it.
The .l10n.php format is a performance answer to .mo parsing: a PHP array that opcache can retain across requests.
Locale switching reloads all textdomains, so switching in a loop (for example a per-recipient email loop) pays a full reload per iteration.

modules.name: formatting-and-sanitization
modules.purpose: Text transformation on the way in and out: escaping, sanitizing, typographic transformation and slashing. At 350 KB, formatting.php is the single largest file in WordPress.

functions.name: esc_url_raw
functions.note: no & encoding — for storage and redirects

business_rules.description: Escaping is applied at output and chosen by context; there is no single universal escaper.
esc_url() encodes & to & for use in markup; esc_url_raw() does not, for storage and Location headers.
wpautop() and wptexturize() run on the_content output, not on stored content, which is why the database holds plain newlines.
Both wpautop() and wptexturize() skip a maintained list of block-level and code tags.
All superglobal input is slashed by wp_magic_quotes(); wp_unslash() is required before use.
sanitize_title() produces a URL-safe slug; sanitize_key() lowercases and restricts to [a-z0-9_-].
sanitize_option() dispatches per option name and is applied on every option write.

algorithms.name: context-specific output escaping
algorithms.description: A distinct escaper per output context (HTML text, attribute, URL-in-markup, raw URL, JS, textarea, XML), applied at render rather than at storage.

algorithms.name: regex typographic transformation
algorithms.description: wpautop and wptexturize transform rendered HTML with regular expressions while maintaining skip-lists for block-level and code tags.

findings.finding: A 350 KB file mixing escaping, sanitizing, typography and slashing is the largest single grab-bag in core and is loaded on every request.
The escape-at-output discipline is WordPress's primary XSS defense but is a convention enforced by review, not by the type system or the API.
esc_url() and esc_url_raw() differ by one character of output and are used in different contexts; the naming does not signal which is which.
Regex-based HTML transformation in wpautop and wptexturize is exactly what the HTML API replaced elsewhere, yet both still run on every rendered post.
The universal slashing convention has no compile-time or runtime enforcement; a missing wp_unslash() produces visible corruption rather than an error.

modules.name: kses-security
modules.purpose: KSES Strips Evil Scripts: an HTML allowlist filter and the last line of defense for untrusted markup.

business_rules.description: KSES is an allowlist: anything not explicitly permitted is stripped.
22 protocols are allowed by default.
The protocol list is memoized in a static and filterable only before wp_loaded, freezing it for the rest of the request.
Scheme comparison decodes entities, strips whitespace, removes null bytes and lowercases before matching the allowlist.
Colons are recognized as ':', ':', ':' and ':'.
Truncated colon entities are repaired before splitting so they cannot evade detection.
A feed: prefix triggers re-examination of the remainder, capped at 2 levels of recursion.
A disallowed scheme yields an empty protocol string, leaving the URL schemeless rather than passing it through.
Allowlists are context-specific: post, strip, data, entities, user_description, pre_user_description.
Entity normalization converts all & to & before selectively restoring valid named and numeric entities.

algorithms.name: four-step scheme normalization
algorithms.description: Decode entities, strip whitespace, remove null bytes, lowercase; each step answers a specific historical XSS bypass technique before the allowlist comparison.

algorithms.name: multi-encoding colon detection
algorithms.description: preg_split on ':' plus its numeric, hex and named entity encodings, with a prior repair pass for truncated colon entities.

algorithms.name: depth-capped nested scheme recursion
algorithms.description: feed: is allowed, so what follows it is re-examined recursively with a hard cap of 2 levels, defeating feed:javascript: while keeping feed: support.

findings.finding: The four-step scheme normalization is a catalogue of two decades of XSS bypass attempts, each line answering a specific historical technique; the most attack-informed code in WordPress after wp_http_validate_url().
The feed: recursion with a hard depth cap shows the nested-scheme attack was found in the wild and fixed without removing feed: support.
Freezing the protocol allowlist at wp_loaded is a rare temporal security boundary: the same filter behaves differently depending on when it runs.
KSES only applies where it is called; content saved by a user with unfiltered_html bypasses it entirely, making it a capability-gated defense rather than a universal one.
KSES parses HTML with regular expressions while the HTML API exists in the same codebase; it has not been migrated and is the higher-risk of the two.

modules.name: error-handling-and-recovery-mode
modules.purpose: Survive a fatal PHP error: catch it, identify which plugin or theme caused it, pause that extension, and email the administrator a link to a mode where the site loads without it.

fields.name: errors
fields.note: multiple codes, each with multiple messages

business_rules.description: WP_Error holds multiple codes each with multiple messages; get_error_message() returns only the first.
Only E_ERROR, E_PARSE, E_USER_ERROR, E_COMPILE_ERROR and E_RECOVERABLE_ERROR trigger the fatal error handler; warnings and notices do not.
The wp_should_handle_php_error filter can opt additional error types in.
A wp-content/fatal-error-handler.php drop-in replaces the error template.
The handler is registered before the database connects, so DB failures remain recoverable.
The offending extension is identified from the error's file path and recorded in paused-extensions storage.
The recovery email is rate-limited to once per day, filterable via recovery_mode_email_rate_limit.
The recovery link TTL is max(filtered_ttl, rate_limit), so the link can never expire before another email may be sent.
The recovery cookie is httponly, secure when is_ssl(), and set on both COOKIEPATH and SITECOOKIEPATH.
Paused extensions are skipped at boot until the administrator exits recovery mode.

algorithms.name: detect-attribute-pause-recover loop
algorithms.description: register_shutdown_function catches the fatal, the error's file path maps to a plugin or theme, the extension is stored as paused, an email with a signed link is sent, and the boot sequence skips the paused extension on subsequent requests.

algorithms.name: lockout-proof TTL constraint
algorithms.description: get_link_ttl() returns max(filtered_ttl, rate_limit) so a misconfigured filter cannot make links expire faster than replacements can be sent.

findings.finding: The full loop (detect, attribute, pause, skip, notify, recover) is genuinely well engineered and unusual in a CMS, converting a white screen of death into a degraded but usable site.
max(ttl, rate_limit) is a small guard preventing an administrator lockout that no amount of filter misconfiguration can produce: defensive design against the extension API rather than against users.
Extension attribution is by file path, so an error thrown inside core but caused by a plugin's data is attributed to core and the wrong extension is paused.
WP_Error and WP_Exception coexist with no migration deadline; two error models are in simultaneous use across the codebase.
Fatal-error handling is itself a drop-in, so a site can replace the mechanism that catches its own fatal errors.

modules.name: performance-speculation-view-transitions
modules.purpose: Modern browser-performance primitives: the Speculation Rules API for prefetch and prerender, plus View Transitions.

business_rules.description: Speculation mode is prefetch or prerender; eagerness is conservative, moderate or eager.
Core defaults to prefetch with conservative eagerness, the most cautious combination.
Hosting providers may override the default configuration via a documented override path.
URL patterns are prefixed for subdirectory installs by WP_URL_Pattern_Prefixer.
Rules are emitted as a speculationrules JSON script block.
View Transitions support in this release is limited to admin CSS plus a configuration surface.

algorithms.name: two-axis speculation configuration
algorithms.description: mode (prefetch vs prerender) crossed with eagerness (conservative, moderate, eager), defaulting to the least aggressive pair, with a hosting-provider override channel.

findings.finding: prefetch plus conservative as the default is correct: prerender runs the target page's scripts speculatively, which would distort analytics and trigger side effects for pages never visited.
An explicit hosting-provider override channel is unusual in core, which normally recognizes only site owners and plugin authors as configuration actors.
View Transitions ships infrastructure ahead of the feature: config classes exist before there is much to configure.

modules.name: admin-application
modules.purpose: The /wp-admin/ application: 95 screen files, 106 shared includes, 30 network screens, 10 per-user screens, plus the menu system, list tables and admin-ajax.

business_rules.description: WP_ADMIN is defined by admin.php; WP_NETWORK_ADMIN and WP_USER_ADMIN distinguish the three admin contexts.
auth_redirect() at admin.php line 104 is the single authentication gate for every admin screen.
admin_init fires after the admin bootstrap and before any screen-specific code.
wp_scheduled_delete and delete_expired_transients are re-scheduled on admin load if absent.
A db_upgraded option triggers the upgrade path on admin load.
admin-ajax.php dispatches on $_REQUEST['action'] to wp_ajax_{action} or wp_ajax_nopriv_{action}.
Registering a wp_ajax_nopriv_* handler makes that action publicly callable with no further gate; each handler must check capabilities and nonces itself.
WP_List_Table subclasses implement prepare_items() and per-column methods.

algorithms.name: shared bootstrap gate
algorithms.description: admin.php defines the admin context constants, loads WordPress, requires the admin includes, and calls auth_redirect() once before firing admin_init, so every screen inherits authentication.

algorithms.name: action-name ajax dispatch
algorithms.description: $_REQUEST['action'] selects wp_ajax_{action} for logged-in users or wp_ajax_nopriv_{action} for anonymous ones; the nopriv variant IS the authorization model.

findings.finding: Admin-Ajax has no declarative authorization; compared to REST's permission_callback, every ajax action must remember its own capability and nonce check. The most common source of WordPress privilege-escalation CVEs.
One screen per file with 95 files and no controller layer means routing is the filesystem, so there is no central place to enforce a policy across admin screens.
WP_List_Table is officially private and universally extended; documentation and reality diverge completely.
The admin re-schedules missing cron events on load, quietly repairing a broken cron option, but only if an administrator visits.

modules.name: filesystem-api
modules.purpose: Write files portably, including on hosts where PHP cannot write directly and must go through FTP or SSH; plus Ed25519 verification of update packages.

business_rules.description: The FS_METHOD constant overrides all detection.
Direct writing requires that files PHP creates have the same owner as WordPress's own files, not merely that writing succeeds.
$allow_relaxed_file_ownership bypasses the ownership check for contexts where the risk is acceptable.
The chosen direct-method rationale is recorded in $GLOBALS['_wp_filesystem_direct_method'] as 'file_owner' or 'relaxed_ownership'.
Fallback order is direct, then ssh2, then ftpext, then ftpsockets.
A non-existent target directory (such as WP_LANG_DIR) causes the write probe to test its parent instead.
Missing sodium_crypto_sign_verify_detached or sha384 yields signature_verification_unsupported, not a verification failure.
When the sodium extension is absent, the pure-PHP polyfill is speed-tested via runtime_speed_test(100, 10) and rejected if too slow.
Signatures whose decoded length is not SODIUM_CRYPTO_SIGN_BYTES are skipped and counted.
Packages are hashed with SHA-384 and verified against wp_trusted_keys() using Ed25519 detached signatures.
PclZip is the pure-PHP fallback when ZipArchive is unavailable.

algorithms.name: ownership-based method detection
algorithms.description: Write a temp file, compare fileowner() of that file with fileowner() of a WordPress file; only if they match is direct writing used. 'Can write' and 'should write' are treated as different questions.

algorithms.name: degradable signature verification
algorithms.description: Missing crypto yields 'unsupported' rather than 'invalid' so old hosts can still update; the pure-PHP polyfill is speed-tested first to avoid exhausting max_execution_time.

findings.finding: The ownership check is thoughtful shared-hosting security: 'can write' and 'should write' are different questions and WordPress asks the second.
Signature verification degrading to 'unsupported' means a host without sodium installs updates unverified; availability was deliberately chosen over integrity.
The polyfill speed test is a rare case of runtime performance measurement gating a security operation.
Four filesystem backends means every update-path file operation is written against an abstraction whose FTP implementations are exercised on a small fraction of installs.

modules.name: updates-and-upgrader
modules.purpose: Check for, download, verify and install core, plugin, theme and translation updates, and migrate the database schema between versions.

business_rules.description: Update data is cached in the update_core, update_plugins and update_themes site transients.
The check timeout escalates: 1 minute during cron, 1 hour after a recent attempt, 2 hours, then 12 hours in steady state.
A re-check is suppressed within 12 hours of last_checked.
Packages are signature-verified after download and before extraction.
The site enters maintenance mode for the duration of install_package().
Core updates use update-core.php, which carries per-version file manifests so obsolete files can be removed.
Schema migrations are version-gated upgrade_NNN() functions applied in sequence from the site's current db version.
dbDelta() diffs the declared CREATE TABLE schema against the live schema and emits the necessary ALTER statements.
$wp_db_version in version.php is the single schema version marker.

algorithms.name: escalating check backoff
algorithms.description: Timeout rises from 1 minute during cron through 1 hour and 2 hours to 12 hours in steady state, so a failing update endpoint costs one slow request per hour rather than one per page view.

algorithms.name: diff-based schema migration
algorithms.description: dbDelta() compares wp_get_db_schema()'s CREATE TABLE statements with the live schema and emits ALTER statements; data migrations that cannot be expressed as schema shape live in version-gated upgrade_NNN() functions.

algorithms.name: download-verify-unpack-install pipeline
algorithms.description: download_package with signature verification, unpack via ZipArchive or PclZip, install_package under maintenance mode, with per-version file manifests for core cleanup.

findings.finding: The escalating timeout is a well-judged backoff: a failing update endpoint costs a site one slow request per hour rather than one per page view.
dbDelta() infers migrations by diffing rather than recording them; it cannot express data migrations, only schema shape, which is why upgrade_NNN() functions exist alongside it.
Auto-updates plus maintenance mode plus paused extensions plus recovery mode compose into a resilient update story, each mechanism covering a different failure mode of the others.
Core knows the file manifest of every prior version in order to clean up, and that list is hand-maintained in update-core.php.

modules.name: site-health
modules.purpose: Run diagnostic tests and surface configuration problems, with a debug-data collector for support.

business_rules.description: Tests are either direct (run synchronously during page load) or async (fetched by JavaScript), so slow tests do not block the page.
Test statuses are good, recommended and critical.
WP_Site_Health is instantiated during boot specifically so its cron events can fire.
The loopback test is how a site detects that WP-Cron cannot self-invoke.
Results are also exposed through the site-health REST controller.

algorithms.name: direct/async test split
algorithms.description: Tests are partitioned so that expensive checks (loopback HTTP, remote version checks) run asynchronously via JavaScript after page load.

findings.finding: Site Health is the only place core systematically checks its own operating assumptions: that cron can spawn, that HTTPS works, that the REST API is reachable.
Instantiating a diagnostic class on every request purely to keep a cron event registered is a small but real site-wide cost paid for an admin feature.

modules.name: multisite
modules.purpose: Run many sites from one installation, sharing users and a codebase while separating content.

business_rules.description: Each site gets its own prefixed table set (wp_{blog_id}_posts etc.); users and usermeta are shared network-wide.
switch_to_blog() maintains a stack and must be paired with restore_current_blog().
Switching a blog changes $wpdb's table prefix and the object cache's blog prefix together.
Role membership is per site, stored as {prefix}capabilities user meta, so one user row carries many role assignments.
Super admins sit above the role system and bypass every capability check except do_not_allow.
The sunrise.php drop-in loads before network resolution, enabling domain mapping.
Network-activated plugins load before muplugins_loaded.
Site and network options live in wp_blogmeta and wp_sitemeta respectively.

algorithms.name: table-prefix site isolation
algorithms.description: Blog-scoped tables are prefixed per blog id while users, usermeta and the ms-global tables are shared; set_blog_id() recomputes only the blog-scoped names.

algorithms.name: stacked blog switching
algorithms.description: switch_to_blog pushes onto a stack and updates wpdb prefix, object cache blog prefix and assorted globals; restore_current_blog pops. An unbalanced switch corrupts every subsequent query.

findings.finding: Table-per-site means a 1000-site network has roughly 11000 tables; schema migrations must run per site and dbDelta() is invoked once per blog.
switch_to_blog() changes global state and must be unwound manually; an unbalanced switch corrupts every subsequent query in the request.
Multisite is not a layer on top of WordPress but is_multisite() branches threaded through the kernel: wpdb, the object cache, capabilities, options and boot all behave differently.
Shared users with per-site roles is the right model but means user meta grows linearly with the number of sites a user belongs to.

modules.name: deprecated-compat
modules.purpose: Keep code written for WordPress 1.5 working on WordPress 7.2, and polyfill newer PHP functions so core can use modern syntax on PHP 7.4.

business_rules.description: Deprecated functions remain fully functional; only a debug-time notice is added.
Deprecation notices appear only when WP_DEBUG is enabled, so they are invisible in production.
Deprecated hooks still fire, warning only if a callback is actually registered.
Old file paths are preserved as aliases (class.wp-scripts.php alongside class-wp-scripts.php) because plugins require them directly.
compat.php and php-compat/ polyfill newer PHP functions so core can use modern syntax while supporting PHP 7.4.
Nothing in the deprecated layer has a removal date.

algorithms.name: functional deprecation
algorithms.description: The deprecated function keeps working and merely calls _deprecated_function(), which emits a notice only under WP_DEBUG.

algorithms.name: listener-gated hook deprecation
algorithms.description: apply_filters_deprecated()/do_action_deprecated() emit their notice only when a callback is registered, so unused deprecated hooks stay silent.

findings.finding: 9112 lines of compatibility code is not technical debt but the product decision that made WordPress ubiquitous: a site from 2008 still upgrades.
Preserving filenames as public API is the strongest statement of the compatibility commitment in the codebase.
Nothing is ever removed and nothing has a sunset date, so the compatibility surface only grows; every deprecated function is also a permanently supported one.
Deprecation notices are invisible in production, so a plugin can rely on deprecated APIs indefinitely without its users ever seeing a warning.
